title: The SCIP Optimization Suite 4.0
contribution: A group release report for SCIP Optimization Suite 4.0 (SCIP 4.0, SoPlex 3.0, UG, GCG, SCIP-Jack, PolySCIP, SCIP-SDP) that presents implementation changes and their computational consequences, ending each feature with a default decision tied to a measurement, plus small algorithmic results (cycle bounds, KKT reformulation, LVB generalisation, row/column basis lemma); no code is credited to Gleixner (p. 74).
problem_entry: Release report, not a research question: a snapshot of the development process (pp. 3-4); features enter from observed misbehaviour or motivating applications (toy instance for cycle detection p. 9, propagation-loop side effect pp. 12-13, line planning p. 10, supply networks pp. 11-12, over-tuning risk p. 16).
key_idea: Each feature ends with a default decision tied to a measurement: off when no gain (cycle detection p. 9, NLOBBT p. 36, gauge/projection separators pp. 38-39, polishing p. 49), on when neutral or better (dual-ray analysis p. 28, row basis switch p. 56); randomization parameters (Table 1, p. 17) and deterministic concurrent solver (pp. 39-42).
assumptions: CIP framework (MINLP, MIQCP, MBQP, MIP) with linear objective (pp. 4-5); assumptions stated where arguments are given (bounded feasible set pp. 29-30, Slater p. 35, RELAX_INCLUDESLP p. 15, interior point p. 37); libraries MMM, MIPLIB 2010, MINLPLib2 subsets, QP sets, 215 LPs (pp. 14-72); no exact or rational arithmetic anywhere.
proof_devices: v-bound aggregation along a cycle giving infeasibility or bound beta/(1-alpha) (pp. 8-9)
clique partitioning by connected components first (p. 10)
KKT-based MBQP to MBPCC equivalence (pp. 29-30)
Lagrangian variable bound from KKT and convexity, generalising Gleixner-Weltge [72] (pp. 34-36)
Lemma 4.1 row/column basis regularity via determinants (p. 55)
Farkas proof constraint reused for propagation (pp. 27-28)
gauge binary search and projection via eigendecomposition plus Newton (pp. 37-39)
power-of-2 scaling (p. 46)
persistent scaling interface layer (p. 47)
NLP tolerance 10^-8 vs 10^-6 for NLOBBT bounds (p. 36)
MOSEK tolerance conversion (p. 68)
deterministic clock fitted by Lasso with leave-one-instance-out CV (p. 41)
delayed communication-point reading (Fig. 5, p. 42)
experiments: Feature on/off in one build on MMM with five seeds (solved = all seeds, seed-spread variability 7.6% to 5.5%, p. 14), leave-one-out heuristics (p. 25), affected subsets (pp. 28, 56), separator netting (p. 39); release SCIP 4.0 vs 3.2.1 on MIPLIB 2010 and 115 MINLPLib2 with four permutations, 'failed' column (pp. 70-73); text-table mismatches pp. 31-34; no significance test.
positioning: Continues SCIP 3.2 report [63]; beside CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, Cbc, SYMPHONY (pp. 4-5); credits reused ideas (Achterberg et al. [4] p. 20, patent [3] p. 48, Fischetti et al. p. 40, Elhallaoui et al. pp. 45, 49); Gleixner's own work only as cited sources [70]-[72] (pp. 34-35, 54).
writing: Per-feature template (motivation, feature description, computational results, default status); explicit local hedges (pp. 12, 37, 51, 53, 57); some causal attributions beyond data (pp. 59, 63, 72); per-section code contributions paragraph (p. 74).
limits_future: Results 'only a rough indication' (p. 70); de-tuning bias ~11% default vs ~2% over permutations (p. 71); MINLP solved count falls, read as 3.2.1 over-tuning (p. 72); future: compare with seeds not permutations (p. 71), reduce separator effort (p. 39), DBDS targets (p. 54), UG sharing (p. 58), PolySCIP (pp. 66-67).

title: Verifying Integer Programming Results
contribution: Proposes a certificate format (VIPR) for MIP results as a flat list of statements each checked by a few inference rules (linear inference, rounding, assumption, unsplitting), with reference software (exact rational checker, tightener, viewer), certificate output from a modified exact rational SCIP, and a computational demonstration on 107 instances.
problem_entry: MIP software can return wrong results (floating point, and programming errors in exact solvers); formal verification too ambitious, MIP certificates not obvious, solvers hide trees and cuts, current practice is cross-solver comparison or solution checking; applications circuit verification and Frankl's conjecture (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Flatten the branch-and-bound tree into a bottom-up list of derived constraints justified by linear inequality inference, rounding (CG cuts), assumptions and unsplitting; the checker deduces assumption lists on the fly; general disjunctions and split cuts representable; price: no direct reading of leaves (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: MILP with rational data, specified and solved in exact rational arithmetic (p. 5); split disjunction branching and cuts derivable as split cuts (p. 6); easy (57) and hard (50) sets of Cook, Koch, Steffy, Wolter [13] (p. 9; Table 1, p. 10).
proof_devices: linear inequality inference via LP duality (p. 5)
rounding rule for integral left-hand sides (p. 6)
assumption and unsplitting rules (pp. 7-8)
split cuts via assume, derive both sides, unsplit (Remark 3, p. 8)
viprchk exact rational checker with GMP (p. 8)
viprttn dependency-graph tightening with DFS topological sort (pp. 8-9)
vipr2html viewer (p. 8)
last-referencing index stored per derived constraint for early memory freeing (p. 8)
hybrid producer: CPLEX floating-point LP plus QSopt_ex exact LP, Project-and-shift and Exact LP certificates (p. 9)
experiments: 107 instances, exclusive Xeon jobs, 1 h and 10 GB certificate cap; arms SCIP, SCIP+C, VIPR; categories all/solved/memout/timeout, shifted geometric means (p. 9); certificate run ~2.1x (easy) and ~1.8x (hard), checking about half/quarter of the solve, I/O ~7%, 17 memouts, tightening >50%, markshare1_1 10 GB to 8 kB (Table 1, p. 10); no significance test, no second checker.
positioning: Against formal code verification (p. 3) and cross-solver comparison or the MIPLIB checker (p. 4); simpler than Applegate et al. and Carr et al.; first public general MIP certificate software 'To the best of our knowledge' (pp. 4-5); borrows from SAT proof checking, DRAT-trim, Hooker's inference duality (pp. 4-5); safe bounds and safe Gomory cuts as related (pp. 3, 10).
writing: Conceptual paper, file spec moved to the repository (p. 5); builds LP to IP to branch and cut with worked Examples 1-3 (pp. 5-8); explicit hedges (pp. 3-4); enumerated observations (pp. 9-10); 'significantly' without a test (p. 10); 'the first step of many' (p. 10).
limits_future: Certificates only for two dual-bounding methods, producer available on request, 17 memouts, redundant output with two named fixes (pp. 9-10); forecast closer to plain exact SCIP since I/O ~7% (p. 10); future: floating-point certificates via directed rounding and interval arithmetic, approximate certificates for debugging and measuring numerical violation, HOL Light (pp. 10-11); unwritten: presolve, propagation and conflict analysis not exercised, no test of the checker.

transferable: Write a certificate as a flat list of derived constraints, each justified by one rule (sign-constrained linear combination, rounding, assumption, unsplitting), so the checker needs no knowledge of the producing algorithm (pp. 5-8).

Flatten a branch-and-bound tree into a bottom-up derivation: branching constraints enter as assumptions, pairs of contradictions are unsplit, and the checker tracks assumption lists on the fly (pp. 7-8).
Represent split cuts the same way: assume each side, derive the cut on both, unsplit (p. 8).
Store the last referencing index after each statement so checkers can free memory (p. 8).
Trim a naively printed certificate with a dependency-graph pass that keeps only the component reaching the final claim (p. 9).
Report overhead on both-solved instances and file runs that hit the memory or time cap in their own rows (p. 9).
Measure the I/O share of an overhead before forecasting how far it can shrink (p. 10).
coauthors: Kevin K. H. Cheung, Daniel E. Steffy

quotes.text: We again emphasize that the format was designed with simplicity in mind; the certificate verification program we have provided is merely a reference and others should be able to write their own verifiers without much difficulty.
